summary: Describes using AES Counter Mode with an explicit initialization vector to encrypt IKEv2 exchanges that follow the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A way of scrambling IPsec setup messages with a certain lock, using a fresh starting value each time.

questions: using aes counter mode with ike
how to use aes-ctr with ikev2
subtitle: A fast encryption method for protecting IKEv2 key exchange messages

tldr.problem: IKEv2 needed a recommended encryption method that was faster than the mandatory algorithms while maintaining security.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5930 specifies how to use AES in Counter Mode (AES-CTR), an encryption approach that converts a cipher into a stream cipher, to protect the IKEv2 messages that follow the initial key agreement.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now use AES-CTR for IKEv2 encryption, gaining performance improvements, but implementers must be careful about counter mode risks.

today: RFC 5930 is an Informational specification published in July 2010 and has not been obsoleted. It defines the usage of AES-CTR for IKEv2 encryption, though implementers often use other faster or simpler algorithms for key exchange protection.

sections.title: What AES-CTR is and Why It Matters
sections.content:
RFC 5930 explains how to use AES Counter Mode (AES-CTR) with IKEv2, the protocol that sets up and manages IPsec security associations. IKEv2 is how two systems negotiate encryption keys and agree on how to protect their traffic.

AES-CTR is an encryption mode where the AES algorithm generates a stream of random-looking bytes, which are mixed with the plaintext message to encrypt it. This differs from block cipher modes that encrypt fixed-size blocks at a time. RFC 4307 recommended that IKEv2 implementations SHOULD support AES-CTR, but no document explained how to do it. This RFC fills that gap.

The main advantage is speed: counter mode can encrypt data faster than some other modes, and it does not require padding. However, counter mode also carries specific security risks if implemented incorrectly, so implementers must understand those risks before deploying it.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 is how two computers agree on secret codes to protect their messages. AES-CTR is a way to scramble information super fast using a counter that generates new encryption bytes for each part of the message. This RFC says how to do that safely.

sections.title: The Encrypted Payload Structure
sections.content:
When AES-CTR is used in IKEv2, it encrypts the payload (the message content) following the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange. The encrypted payload contains two unencrypted fields and one encrypted section.

The initialization vector (IV), which must be 8 octets (bytes) when using AES-CTR, is sent in the clear. The IV is a starting value that ensures each message produces different ciphertext even with the same key. The integrity checksum data is also unencrypted, allowing the receiver to verify the message was not tampered with in transit. Both of these fields are required by IKEv2 regardless of the encryption method used.

When AES-CTR is used, the RFC specifies that no padding should be added to the encrypted data, and the Pad Length field should be zero. The receiver must still accept any padding that results in proper alignment, as allowed by RFC 4306, but under normal circumstances padding is unnecessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The message starts with a fresh starting number (the IV) and a checking number, both sent openly. Then the secret part gets scrambled using AES-CTR, with no need to add extra filler bytes at the end.

sections.title: How the Counter Block Works
sections.content:
At the heart of AES-CTR is the counter block, a 128-bit structure that AES processes to generate the encryption stream. The counter block has three parts: a 4-octet (32-bit) nonce derived from the key material, the 8-octet IV, and a 4-octet block counter that starts at one and increments by one for each block.

To encrypt a message, the counter block is fed into the AES algorithm repeatedly. The first iteration uses counter value 1, the second uses counter value 2, and so on. Each iteration produces 128 bits of key stream. These key stream blocks are XORed with the plaintext to produce the ciphertext. To decrypt, the same process is repeated to regenerate the key stream, which is XORed with the ciphertext to recover the plaintext.

This design has the advantage that encryption and decryption are identical operations, and no padding is needed because the key stream is arbitrary in length. However, it also means that reusing the same nonce and IV with the same key would produce identical key streams and completely compromise security, so implementations must ensure the IV is never repeated with the same key.
sections.plainLanguage: The counter is like a music box that plays 128 bits of encryption music each time you turn the crank. You start at position 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Each output gets mixed with the message to scramble it. If you ever use the same starting point twice with the same key, someone can figure out your secrets.

sections.title: Negotiation and Setup
sections.content:
The use of AES-CTR with IKEv2 is negotiated in the same way as AES-CTR with ESP (the Encapsulating Security Payload). During the IKEv2 handshake, the two endpoints exchange proposals of which algorithms they support. If both support AES-CTR (identified by the Transform ID ENCR_AES_CTR, which IANA assigned the value 13), it can be selected.

Once AES-CTR is negotiated, the key material is derived in the same way as for AES-CTR in ESP. The key material contains both the actual encryption key (which can be 128, 192, or 256 bits depending on the key size agreed upon) and the nonce value mentioned above. Both are derived from the shared secret using the negotiated pseudo-random function.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers talk to set up IKEv2, they tell each other which encryption methods they can use. If both say yes to AES-CTR (method number 13), they pick it and generate the actual keys and numbers needed.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that security considerations from RFC 3686 (which specifies AES-CTR for ESP) apply directly to AES-CTR in IKEv2. The most critical concern is that AES has a 128-bit block size. After 2^64 blocks are encrypted with a single key, the ciphertext becomes statistically distinguishable from random. However, IKEv2 security associations cannot carry enough data to reach this limit because of message ID constraints, so this theoretical risk does not apply in practice.

Integrity protection is mandatory for IKEv2 security associations, and IKEv2 never reuses static keys. These properties mean that several risks inherent to counter mode in other contexts (static key reuse, lack of integrity) are mitigated. The implementer's responsibility is to never reuse the same IV with the same key and to correctly implement the counter block structure.

The RFC also notes that performance improvements from AES-CTR in the context of IKEv2 are minimal compared to the mandatory-to-implement algorithms, so the choice to deploy it should be made carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest danger is using the same starting point twice—that breaks everything. But IKEv2 is designed so that never happens. Using AES-CTR may not even make things much faster than the standard methods, so you should think hard before using it.
